title: Rate limiter service
summary: A shared limiter that 50 API servers consult a million times a second: the algorithm, atomic counters in Redis, a 5 ms budget, and an outage that must not take the APIs down with it.
interviewerPrompt: Our public API runs on a fleet of servers, and we need to rate-limit callers: things like 100 requests a minute per user. Design the rate limiter. How would you approach it?

clarifyingQuestions.question: What limits do we need to enforce?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Rules such as 100 requests per minute per user and 10,000 requests per minute per API key. Every request carries both a user ID and an API key. Product teams add and change rules a few times a week.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How much traffic?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: About 1M requests per second at peak across a fleet of 50 API servers. Assume peak is twice the daily average.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must limits be exact across the fleet, or is per-server enough?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: They must hold across all servers. A user who spreads requests over the fleet must not get 50 times their limit. Small overshoot of a few percent is acceptable.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How much latency can the check add?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: At most 5 ms at p99 per request.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What does a rejected caller see?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: HTTP 429 with a clear message and a hint for when to retry.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if the limiter itself is down?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The API must keep working. An outage of the limiter must not become an outage of the API.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do bursts matter, or only the per-minute total?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The rule is stated per minute. A user should not be able to send 200 requests in two seconds by straddling a minute boundary.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is this one region or several?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: One region today. We plan a second and third region next year, and per-key limits should then still mean roughly the same thing globally.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are some limits more important than others?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. A few rules protect against abuse, such as login attempts per account. Those matter more than ordinary fairness limits.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do callers need to see their remaining quota?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, in response headers on every request.

deepDiveQuestions: Which algorithm: fixed window, sliding log, sliding-window counter, token bucket or leaky bucket, and what does each cost in memory and accuracy?
How do you keep counters correct when 50 servers update them at once: Redis, Lua scripts and atomicity?
Where does the limiter run: a library in each API server, a sidecar, or a separate service, and how does that fit a 5 ms budget?
What happens when Redis is slow or down: fail open or fail closed?
How do limits hold across several regions?

requestTypes.name: Limit check (user + API key) on every API request

runChallenge.title: 1M checks a second with a zone down
runChallenge.description: Run at the 1M requests/s peak and lose the busiest availability zone after 10 s. Every API request must still get its limit check: at least 990k checks/s with under 0.1% errors, a p99 under 15 ms for the whole path to Redis, and no single point of failure.

commonMistakes: Keeping counters in each API server's memory, so a user spread over 50 servers gets up to 50 times their limit.
Reading the counter, deciding, then writing it back as separate Redis commands, so two servers both read 99 and both allow request 100 and 101.
Choosing a fixed one-minute window without noticing that a caller can send twice the limit in two seconds across the boundary.
Storing a sliding log of every request timestamp for a 10,000-per-minute key, which costs hundreds of kilobytes per key when two counters would do.
Putting a Redis call with no timeout on the request path, so a slow Redis shard makes every API request slow.
Failing closed on every rule, so a Redis outage rejects all traffic and the limiter takes the API down.
Calling one central counter in a home region from every region, which adds a cross-region round trip far beyond a 5 ms budget.
Using each API server's own clock to pick the window, so servers with skewed clocks count into different windows.
